summary:
Llamita turns NASA satellite fire detections into decisions people can act on, at both global and local scale.

Global: Llamita uses the NASA FIRMS API to query active fires anywhere in the world, by continent, by country or by the visible map area, with history back to 2000. It combines the two FIRMS sensors, MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m), on a common ~1 km grid, so each fire appears as a single point instead of several duplicates. Every merged point keeps the strongest reading and a record of which sensors saw it.

Local: For the Cochabamba challenge, Llamita adds the official geographic layers of the Cochabamba Municipal Government (GAMC) through a secure server-side proxy. It also assigns each hotspot to its province and municipality, so authorities and fire brigades can filter by territory, track trends in the statistics view, and export reports as PDF, Excel, CSV, Shapefile or GeoJSON.

The result is one open-source tool that links planetary-scale satellite monitoring with local decision-making.
details:
What it does and how it works

Llamita is a web app for monitoring wildfires and thermal hotspots. It turns NASA satellite detections into a clear map, statistics and reports. The server queries the NASA FIRMS API by date range, sensor and area: a continent, a country, the visible map or the Cochabamba region. Results come back on an interactive map, with each hotspot sized and colored by its fire radiative power (FRP).

Its core is a harmonization step for MODIS (1 km pixels) and VIIRS (375 m pixels). Detections are placed on a common ~1 km grid calibrated to Cochabamba's latitude, then grouped by Bolivia-local day and grid cell. Each group becomes one record that keeps:

•⁠ ⁠the VIIRS coordinates, which are the more precise ones;

•⁠ ⁠the maximum FRP, not the sum, so overlapping pixels aren't counted twice;

•⁠ ⁠which sensors saw the fire and how many observations were merged.

For the local challenge, Llamita adds the official layers of the Cochabamba Municipal Government (GAMC) through a secure server-side proxy. It also assigns every hotspot to its province and municipality.

Benefits

•⁠ ⁠One fire appears as one point, so counts and statistics are trustworthy.

•⁠ ⁠Anyone can filter by territory, date and sensor without GIS skills.

•⁠ ⁠Reports in PDF, Excel, CSV, Shapefile or GeoJSON, always citing the data source.

•⁠ ⁠API keys stay on the server, and caching protects the FIRMS quota.

Intended impact

Fire brigades, municipal authorities and communities can spot fires earlier, prioritize areas and back their decisions with traceable data. That shortens the time between a satellite detection and action on the ground.

Tools and technologies

•⁠ ⁠Languages: TypeScript, HTML and CSS.

•⁠ ⁠Framework: Next.js 16 and React 19.

•⁠ ⁠Mapping and geodata: Leaflet for the map and Turf for geospatial analysis.

•⁠ ⁠Styling: Tailwind CSS.

•⁠ ⁠Reports: jsPDF, SheetJS and shp-write.

•⁠ ⁠Caching: Redis.

•⁠ ⁠Workflow and deployment: pnpm, ESLint, Prettier, automated tests, Docker, GitHub Actions, and Kubernetes with GitOps.

•⁠ ⁠Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS), GAMC WMS services, geoBoundaries / GeoBolivia boundaries, and OpenStreetMap and Esri basemaps.

•⁠ ⁠Hardware: no special hardware is needed; it runs in any web browser.

Creativity

Llamita works at both global and local scale. Satellite data that covers the whole planet is combined with official municipal layers in one tool. Its harmonization approach (a common grid, maximum FRP and preserved provenance) solves a problem most fire maps ignore: the same fire counted several times. The visual design was created for this project, with a heat scale readable by colorblind users, a dark theme suited to heat maps, and a llama inside a flame as the logo.
